hero.name: Jatin
hero.who: a 21-year-old B.Com student in Jaipur who survives on chai and late nights

story.b: Jatin is in his final year of B.Com in Jaipur. Mornings are college in Malviya Nagar. Evenings he tutors two Class 10 students in maths. From eleven at night to half past two he studies for his own exams, with music playing on his phone. He drinks six cups of chai a day from the stall outside college. He sleeps four or five hours and is quietly proud of it. Sleep, he tells friends, is for people with smaller dreams. But lately things are slipping. He gave a student the wrong answer key. He snapped at his younger sister over the TV remote. And in a cost accounting test, he blanked on a formula he had revised the night before.

ask.q: Jatin thinks sleep is wasted time. Which change in his thinking would help most?
o: He just needs stronger chai to get through the busy months
Sleep is part of the work, because a rested mind usually works better
He can sleep as much as he likes once his exams are over
ask.why: Stronger chai hides tiredness but does not repay it. Waiting until after exams means months of weaker thinking, mood and health, right when he needs them most. Seeing sleep as part of the work, not a break from it, is the shift that makes every other change possible.

chapters.take: Sleep is not time stolen from your goals. It feeds them.

story.b: Jatin picks a bedtime he can actually keep. Lights out at midnight, alarm at half past seven. To make room, he plans tuition lessons during his free period at college and moves his own study to nine till half past eleven. The first few nights he lies awake, his mind buzzing, sure he is wasting precious hours. By the second week something changes. He stops yawning in the eleven o'clock lecture. He checks his students' homework without mistakes. He does not snap when his sister changes the channel. His mother, frying puris on Sunday morning, says he looks less like a ghost. Jatin laughs, but he notices he is getting more done, not less.

ask.q: A big assignment is due and Jatin wants to skip his new bedtime for a week. What should he do?
o: Skip sleep this week and catch up with one long Sunday nap
Skip sleep, since one week of late nights cannot really hurt
Keep the bedtime and plan the assignment into his earlier hours
ask.why: A week of short nights quietly lowers the very thinking the assignment needs, and one long nap is unlikely to fully make up for it. Keeping the bedtime and moving the work earlier protects both his health and the quality of what he submits.

chapters.take: Guard your sleep first, then fit the work around it.

story.b: The night before the semester's accounts exam, Jatin's friends plan an all-nighter in Manav's room, with energy drinks and a big flask of chai. They invite him. The old Jatin would have gone straight there. This time he revises his notes from seven to ten, works through two past questions, eats dal baati with his family and goes to bed at eleven. In the morning, over a hot kachori, he flips through his notes once more for fifteen minutes. In the exam hall the formulas are simply there, waiting. He writes steadily. Manav, sitting two rows ahead, keeps rubbing his eyes, and afterwards says he could not remember half of what he read at four.

ask.q: The night before an exam, Jatin's friends invite him to an all-night group study. What should he do?
o: Revise in the evening, then sleep and do a quick review in the morning
Join them until dawn, since more hours of study means more marks
Join until three, then sleep for whatever time is left
ask.why: Sleep seems to help lock in what he studied during the day. Cramming till dawn may weaken the very memories he needs, and three hours of sleep cuts that process short. Evening revision plus a full night lets the learning settle, with a light check in the morning.

chapters.take: Study, then sleep. The sleep is part of the studying.

story.b: Jatin notices that Mondays are always the worst. On weekends he watches web series until three and sleeps till noon. By Monday morning he feels like he has flown in from another country. He also knows he is a bit of a night owl, so forcing a five o'clock alarm would never last. Instead, he keeps his times steady all week, lights out around midnight and up by half past seven, even on Sundays, give or take half an hour. At eleven each night he switches off the bright tube light, uses only the small table lamp and turns his phone to its dim night setting. After two weeks, Monday feels just like any other day.

ask.q: Jatin feels groggy every Monday after late weekend nights. What is the best fix?
o: Wake at five on Mondays to shock his body back into shape
Drink extra chai on Mondays to push through the fog
Keep roughly the same sleep times on weekends, with dim lights late
ask.why: Big swings between weekend and weekday times confuse his body clock, so Monday feels like jet lag. A sudden five o'clock alarm swings it again, and extra chai only hides the fog. Steady times and dim evening light help the clock settle.

chapters.take: Your body runs on a clock. Keep its times steady and work with it.

story.b: Jatin counts his chai and finds the last cup usually comes at nine at night, just before study time. He decides his last chai will now be at two in the afternoon. Evenings get warm water and a short walk around the colony instead. The first few nights, he is surprised by how sleepy he feels at ten, as if the tiredness had been waiting behind a door. At a cousin's wedding that month, an uncle tells him a drink at night helps him sleep. Jatin remembers reading that alcohol may make sleep shallower later in the night. He sticks to lassi, dances badly with his cousins, and goes home early.

ask.q: After cutting his evening chai, Jatin feels very sleepy at ten. What does this most likely mean?
o: Cutting chai has made him weak, so he should bring it back
The tiredness was there all along, and the chai was hiding it
He should switch to an energy drink until the sleepiness fades
ask.why: Caffeine blocks the feeling of sleepiness without removing the need for sleep. When the evening chai goes, the hidden tiredness shows up. Bringing it back or switching to energy drinks just covers the signal again, when the honest answer is simply to sleep.

chapters.take: Chai can hide tiredness, but it cannot pay back the sleep you owe.

story.b: Jatin looks at his room as if it belonged to someone else. A streetlight shines through the thin curtain. The phone charges beside his pillow and lights up with every message. Dinner is often at eleven, heavy with parathas. So he makes small changes. He hangs an old thick bedsheet over the curtain. The phone now charges on the study table across the room. He eats dinner by nine. Some nights he still cannot sleep. Instead of tossing for an hour, he gets up, reads a dull economics book under the table lamp, and goes back when his eyes feel heavy. Around this time, his friend Manav admits he has slept badly for months.

ask.q: Manav has struggled to sleep for months, even with good habits. What should Jatin suggest?
o: Keep the simple habits going and also see a doctor about it
Try sleeping pills from the chemist without asking a doctor
Stay in bed longer each night until sleep finally comes
ask.why: Simple habits help many people, but months of poor sleep deserve a doctor's view, since there may be causes habits alone cannot fix. Pills without a prescription can be risky, and lying awake in bed for hours can turn the bed into a place for worry.

chapters.take: Make sleep easy with small habits, and ask a doctor when it stays hard.

story.b: By the time the final exams arrive, Jatin's life has a new shape. He sleeps around midnight and wakes at half past seven, most days. His two cups of chai are finished by two. The bedsheet still hangs over the curtain, and his phone still sleeps on the study table. On exam mornings he eats a kachori, glances at his notes and walks in calm. His results are his best in three years, but his family notices other things first. He laughs with his sister. His tuition students say he explains better. Manav saw a doctor and is slowly sleeping better too. On some wedding nights Jatin still stays up late, then simply gets back on track.

chapters.take: Protect your sleep, and your days get sharper on their own.
